n: The book opens by naming its author as “the Preacher,” a son of David who ruled in Jerusalem. Tradition identifies him with Solomon, the king famous for his wisdom, though many scholars think a later writer used Solomon’s voice.

f.g: Hebrew Qoheleth — one who gathers an assembly and speaks to it; the Greek title Ecclesiastes means the same.

n: This is the book’s theme sentence. “Vanity of vanities” is a Hebrew way of saying “the most fleeting thing of all.” Life lived only for earthly things vanishes like a breath.

f.g: Hebrew hebel — breath, vapor, mist; something brief, empty, or impossible to grasp, not pride.

n: The Preacher asks the question the whole book explores: what lasting gain do people get from all their hard work? “Under the sun” means life viewed from a purely earthly point of view.

f.g: Hebrew yitron — what is left over; lasting gain or advantage.
A phrase used about 29 times in the book: life as seen from the earth alone.

n: People come and go, but the earth stays. Compared with the steady earth, a single human life seems short and small.
The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to rise again. The picture is of endless, tiring repetition that never seems to arrive anywhere new.

f.g: Literally “pants” — like a runner gasping as he hurries back to the starting line.

n: The wind circles south and north and round again. Like the sun, it is busy but keeps returning to the same paths.

f.g: Circular courses; the wind’s regular rounds.

n: Rivers keep pouring into the sea, yet the sea never fills up. Nature illustrates effort that never reaches completion.
Everything is wearisome beyond words. Human desire is never satisfied: our eyes always want to see more and our ears to hear more.

f.g: Or “full of weariness” — everything is tiresome.

n: History repeats itself. What happened before will happen again, and nothing is truly new in human experience when seen only from below.

f.w: no new thing under the sun
f.g: Contrast God’s promise of a “new thing” and a new heaven and earth (Isaiah 43:19; Revelation 21:5).

n: When people think they have found something new, it usually turns out to have existed long before. We simply don’t remember the past well.
Past generations are forgotten, and future ones will be forgotten too. The Preacher feels how quickly human memory fades.
The Preacher introduces himself personally as a king over Israel. What follows is his own report of his search for meaning.
He set out to study everything people do. He calls this search for understanding a heavy task God has given humanity to keep us busy and thinking.
After seeing all human activity, he concludes it is fleeting and like trying to catch the wind.

f.g: Better “striving after wind” or “chasing the wind” — effort that grasps nothing.

n: Some problems simply can’t be fixed by human effort, and what is missing can’t be counted as if it were there. Wisdom has limits.
Talking to himself, the Preacher admits he gained more wisdom than anyone before him in Jerusalem. He had every advantage for this search.

f.g: Thought things through privately; talked with himself.

n: He studied both wisdom and its opposites — madness and foolishness — to understand life fully. Even that study felt like chasing wind.
The more he understood, the more he saw life’s pain and injustice. Knowledge without God’s larger view can bring sorrow rather than peace.

f.g: Wisdom opens one’s eyes to suffering; the book later points to fearing God as the answer (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
